# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-11 10:01 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 262 active entries of tips_notebook.json (50 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier sheets are in history/.

## Everyone
- Ballots are secret, so keep a notepad of every nomination and trial: each player's stated vote, the announced totals and your own. Vote as you said you would and explain any switch first; a mismatch with the totals is a lead, never a hang on its own. (seen in 30 games)
- Totals can be manipulated. A trial total above the voter count means a Ballot Stuffer, and a Fixer silently flips one player's trial votes. Yes/No nomination counts can't be altered, so they are the cleanest liar check. (seen in 2 games)
- A visit shows a destination, not an action. But a corroborated Lookout or Tracker naming X as the only unexplained visitor to a Katana victim is near-proof; don't let 'a visit isn't an attack' acquit X. (seen in 32 games)
- Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit: an unexplained Evil read on a Vanilla claim, a broken visit claim, or a group result where elimination leaves one name. A role-block fully explains a missing result, so that is never a contradiction. (seen in 36 games)
- Each night write your planned target in your will, and post results publicly by day. The result of the night you die never reaches your will. (seen in 29 games)
- Answer a direct question about your night action in one plain sentence the first time it is asked; days of evasion become a case of their own. (seen in 9 games)
- Tokens die with you. Spend one-shot tokens on the first Day or night they can change a vote or remove a threat, and spend a puppet or doubled ballot at least a night before a likely death. (seen in 4 games)

## Village
- Post your role, target and exact result in your first speech after getting it, and counterclaim any copier at once with your full log. Results held back look retrofitted. (seen in 18 games)
- Never announce tonight's target, in public or by PM. A Wiretap may read every PM, and a named target tells blockers and the Katana where to go. (seen in 24 games)
- On Day 2, power roles with no result should not hint at their role or lead loudly. The most organized voice is the usual Night 2 kill. (seen in 24 games)
- Once someone is shown Yakuza mechanically, look at who defended them or pushed to delay their hang. Treat PM links as leads only, since Jesters and Executioners leave trails on purpose. (seen in 30 games)
- Before any hang, ask whether the nominee wins by being hanged. If you must hang a likely Jester, use a bare Guilty majority and keep confirmed power roles on Innocent. (seen in 16 games)
- Hunt Neutral killers deliberately. Read every cause of death, list unwatched Vanilla or unclaimed players and survivors with no protector, and hang the best suspect before the final two, when you can no longer hang them. (seen in 2 games)
- Surviving an attack proves nothing, since Arsonists and Serial Killers have Standard Defense. Ask the survivor at once who protected them. (seen in 17 games)

## Yakuza
- Don't defend a doomed teammate. If your team's votes can't stop the hang, vote Guilty with the town, because hidden Innocent votes show in the totals. (seen in 38 games)
- Send no daytime PMs about team plans, and none to teammates on Day 2; plan in night chat. (seen in 34 games)
- Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours. Never claim or name a Yakuza-only role, and never switch claims once cornered. (seen in 19 games)
- Every member must submit the agreed Katana holder and target every night; one missing vote can cancel the kill. (seen in 20 games)
- Never flatly deny a visit that an FT count, map group or Lookout could expose. Agree a cover in night chat, and move the Katana off any holder a watcher has named. (seen in 22 games)
- After a failed Katana attack, kill or block the likely protector instead of retrying blindly. Prioritize running counts (Fortune Teller, Census Taker) and Party Animals with block logs. (seen in 21 games)
- Use Clerk rigs, puppets and cleans early, but never rig a Day when a teammate is the likely nominee. (seen in 20 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked. If you must explain it, pick one claim at once and never switch. (seen in 6 games)

## Sheriff
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil, so say so whenever you post a Not Evil result. A lone last Yakuza reads Not Evil every night. (seen in 19 games)

## Coroner
- Examine bodies that settle live questions: one side of a duplicate claim, or a hanged suspect. Post the night, target and role in one message the next Day, and skip cleaned bodies. (seen in 3 games)

## Medic
- Use free Standard protection on likely Katana targets, vary your pattern, and never announce targets. Spend a token on self-protection within a night or two of claiming, and never claim you 'saw' a save. (seen in 24 games)

## Vigilante
- Set a trigger by Day 2-3 and fire a Basic shot on a real lead rather than dying with all tokens. A Basic shot that fails without a credible Medic points to innate Defense, so post it. (seen in 11 games)

## Smuggler
- A swap moves only actions aimed at the two swapped players. Aim the Katana at a decoy and swap the decoy with the protected real target, or swap yourself with a Villager to dodge a check. Plan it in night chat rather than vetoing it. (seen in 2 games)

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3 living players are doused, or 2 if you are being questioned. Have a claim ready that explains your douse visits. (seen in 12 games)

rules:
=== PART 1: THE GAME ===

R1 (Overview and winning)
You are playing a Mafia-style game with around 10 players (depending on setup), each in a faction. An omniscient
moderator runs the game. The game alternates Night and Day phases, starting with Night 1: there is no Day 1, so
the first Day is Day 2 (players write their first will before Night 1).
- For most roles, you win iff your faction wins. A faction typically wins iff it has players alive at the end.
- The game ends as soon as all living players, ignoring roles that never block wins, belong to one faction. This is
  checked after every death; deaths that happen together at night are checked together.
- Some Neutral roles never block another faction's win (their role says so); their own wins don't depend on how
  the game ends.

R2 (Factions)
- Village (Good): the largest faction, but with weaker roles and less information.
- Yakuza (Evil): fewer players, stronger roles; they know each other and share a night chat.
- Neutral: each Neutral player is their own one-person faction, even if two players have the same Neutral role.
The list of roles in the game is not public. A role may appear more than once in a game, except these unique
roles, which appear at most once: Smuggler, Vulture.

R15 (Alignments)
Every player has one of three alignments: Good (Village), Evil (Yakuza) or Neutral. Some roles and effects change
how a player's alignment appears; see R19.

R18 (Terms)
- Living players: players who haven't died or left. Every count in these rules ("majority", "random player")
  means living players unless it says otherwise.
- Majority: strictly more than half; exactly half is not a majority.
- Action: anything a role does at night by choice or by its rules (investigating, shooting, blocking, ...).
- Visit: an action on another player counts as A visiting B, unless it is an Astral Visit (R6).
- Astral Visit: an action that is not a visit. Abilities that react to visits (Tracker, Lookout, Trapper,
  Fortune Teller) never see or react to it.
- Alignment check: a result that reports alignment (Sheriff, Seer). See R19 for what they see.
- Exact-role check: a result that reports or tests an exact role (Oracle, Diviner, Ritualist, Mortician, Coroner,
  Talent Agent, a Vigilante's kill).
- Token: a limited-use resource a role starts with. Spent tokens are gone; a role-blocked action spends none.

R11 (The circle)
Players sit in a circle. The dead (and players who leave) are removed from it.

=== PART 2: THE DAY ===

R4 (Day phase, chat, nominations and trials)
Chat:
- There is a public chat and private chats between exactly two players.
- Private messages are not secret: whenever A sends B a private message, everyone sees that A sent B a private
  message, but only A and B see its contents.
Nominations:
- Any player may publicly nominate someone, including themself. All chat stops at once.
- Everyone votes Yes/No at the same time; nobody sees another vote before casting their own. The nominator votes
  Yes by default. There are no abstentions: a player who doesn't vote counts as voting No. Votes are secret: once
  all votes are in, only the number of Yes votes is announced (the nominator is named), never who voted which way.
  Each voter is privately reminded of their own vote.
- If a majority of all votes counted are Yes, the nominee goes on trial.
Trials:
- The nominee says the first public message and may defend themself; others may chat publicly and privately.
  After everyone else has had a turn, the nominee gets one last public message before the vote.
- Then everyone votes Guilty/Innocent at the same time (no abstentions: a player who doesn't vote counts as voting
  Innocent). Votes are secret: only the Guilty and Innocent totals are announced, never who voted which way. Each
  voter is privately reminded of their own vote.
- If a majority of all votes counted are Guilty, the nominee is Executed by Hanging, a Divine Attack, and the Day
  ends immediately.
- If three nominations pass (failed ones don't count) and all three trials end Innocent, the Day ends.
- Some roles can change how votes are counted. If an announced vote total doesn't match the number of voters,
  a role manipulated the count on purpose; it is not an error. One use of such a role can change every trial
  that Day, so the number of changed totals doesn't show how many times a role was used.
Voting Yes or Guilty on yourself is allowed.

R16 (Day length)
Day chat goes around the circle in turns. Each Day the program picks a random living player to speak first;
turns then go around the circle from them in the same order every round. Besides the endings in R4, the Day ends when a full round passes in
which nobody sends a public message or nominates, except that anyone sent a private message during that round
first gets one last turn. The Day also ends after at most 8 rounds.

R22 (Speaking budget)
Day messages and nominations cost speaking budget. Each player earns budget every round of a Day, up to a cap,
and part of what they have left carries into the next Day. A message's price grows with its length and, after
the first rounds of a Day, with the round; private messages cost less than public ones. A nomination costs
budget too. On a trial turn prices are lower and each speaker also gets a trial-only budget, spent first and lost
when the turn ends; the accused's first defense message is free up to a set length. The program sets the
numbers for each game and tells every player at the start.

R23 (Swaps)
Some roles can swap two players for a night. Every action that night aimed at one of them (including the Katana's
attack and automatic actions such as the Ex-Con's visit or the Seer's pair) lands on the other instead, as if its
user had chosen that player. Only the swap itself is not moved (the swapping player's Katana vote is). Results name the player the action's
user chose, so a swapped action's result doesn't show the swap: a Sheriff who checked A learns B's alignment as
A's. A result that lists several players (e.g. a group around the target) is built around B, but A and B trade
places in the list, each named where the other would be; the roles, alignments and counts in it are still the real
players', so the rest of the group can still hint at the swap. A Lookout who watched A watches B instead, and a
Tracker sees the player its target's action landed on. An effect that lasts into the next Day (e.g. listening in
on private messages) follows B, and its user is told at dawn that a swap moved it to B.

R13 (Last wills)
Players may write and update a last will before Night 1, at the beginning of each Day (except those who died the
night before) and during any of their own Day turns. When a player dies, their last will is shared publicly at once.

=== PART 3: THE NIGHT ===

R5 (Night phase)
Chat is off for most players; some (usually a faction, like the Yakuza) have a private night chat. The moderator
wakes players one by one, or faction by faction, to act. When the Night ends, the moderator works out every
effect. By default, effects are announced publicly at the start of the next Day; some are not announced.

R7 (Optional actions)
Every ability is optional ("may") unless its role says "must": any player may choose not to act at Night, not to
use a Day ability, and not to spend a token. Effects a role has automatically, with no choice (e.g. the
Ex-Con's nightly visit), aren't optional, but a role-block still stops them (R9).

R6 (Visits)
- When A performs an action on B, A visits B, unless the action is an Astral Visit.
- A role that targets a player may target itself unless its text says otherwise (e.g. "other than yourself").
- A player whose role can target others but who targets themself shows as visiting themself.
- A player whose action can only affect themself does not show as visiting anyone.
- An action that targets no player (e.g. the Clerk's rig) is not a visit.
- A player who visits the same target with several actions in one night is one visitor to that target: anything
  that lists, counts or reacts to visitors (a watch, a Veteran's alert, a trap) treats them once.

R9 (Role-blocks)
A role-blocked player's actions that night have no effect, exactly as if they had chosen not to act: no visit,
no tokens spent. It lasts only that one night (not the next Day or later nights). Role-blocked players are told
they were role-blocked. Any player can be role-blocked unless their role says otherwise; blocking a player who
has no night action, or who chose not to act, has no other effect, but they are still told. A role-blocker learns
only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked.
A result a role gets with no action at all (its text says "This needs no action") isn't an action, so a role-block
doesn't stop it; automatic actions, such as the Ex-Con's visit or the Seer's random pair, are stopped (R7).

R10 (Simultaneous night resolution)
All night actions happen at the same time. Think of it as two steps: first everyone attempts their actions,
then all results happen together. So investigations that give their result at the end of the night (e.g. the
Seer's random pair) draw from and report on everyone alive when the night began, including players who die that
night.

R21 (Effects that outlast their user)
An effect set up at night for the following Day (e.g. a Clerk's rig, a Prosecutor's prosecution) still happens if
its user dies that night, unless it needs its user to act during that Day (e.g. a Puppeteer writing the puppet's
messages, a Ballot Stuffer's doubled vote); those lapse. Any token spent on it is gone either way (R18).

R20 (Night resolution checklist): a summary of the rules above, in the order the moderator applies them.
1. Remove actions of role-blocked players (R9), automatic ones included (the Ex-Con's visit, the Seer's pair).
   Party Animal, Pharmacist, Smuggler and Veteran can't be role-blocked. Swaps (R23) apply before anything else.
2. Work out who visits whom (R6), including the Katana holder's visit (R8) and the Ex-Con's random visit.
3. Attacks: each kills iff its level beats the target's Defense (R3). Defenses don't stack; the highest counts.
   Traps hit non-Village visitors (Trapper).
4. Results for investigators, using the visits and appearances (R19).
5. Notifications: attackers learn whether they succeeded, attacked players learn the attacking role (R3, with the
   Katana exception in R8), protectors learn nothing (R17), role-blocked players are told (R9), Yakuza learn each
   other's actions (R8).
6. Deaths are revealed at the start of the Day (R12); the win check runs on all of the night's deaths together (R1).

=== PART 4: ATTACKS, DEATH AND INFORMATION ===

R3 (Attack and Defense)
- Levels, lowest to highest: None, Basic, Standard, Strong, Divine. Players have Defense None by default.
- An Attack kills iff its level is strictly higher than the target's Defense.
- Defenses don't stack: a player with several sources of Defense has the highest of them.
- By default the attacker learns whether the Attack succeeded (not the target's Defense), and the target learns
  the role that attacked them (not the attacker's name or Attack level). A target hit by several Attacks in one
  night learns the role behind each, including those that failed. The Katana is an exception (R8).

R17 (Protection feedback)
Protectors (e.g. the Medic) are never told whether their protection stopped an attack, and a protected player is
never told who protected them. A player who is attacked is still told as in R3.

R12 (Death reveals)
When someone dies, their cause of death (e.g. Katana, Vigilante, Execution by Hanging) and last will are revealed
publicly; their role and alignment are not. If several attacks were each fatal, every fatal cause is revealed;
attacks the player survived aren't. The dead leave the circle and can't take part in the game any more. A player
whose win ends their part in the game (a hanged Jester, an Executioner who leaves) is the exception: the
announcement of their win names their role.

R14 (Stall rule)
If a Day begins and nobody has died in the three previous Nights and three previous Days, everyone loses. Deaths
from last Night count even though they're announced today. Every death counts; leaving (like the Executioner's)
doesn't.

R19 (What investigations see)
Alignment checks (Sheriff: Evil / Not Evil; Seer: compares Good / Neutral / Evil) see a player's true alignment,
except:
- Yakuza holding the Katana at the end of the night: Good (Sheriff: Not Evil), even if they died that night.
- Player framed by the Fabricator that night: Evil.
- Ex-Con: Evil.
- Sheriff on Neutrals: Jester and Executioner read Evil; Serial Killer and Arsonist read Not Evil. (Seers see
  every Neutral as Neutral.)
The Census Taker's count is not an alignment check: it always sees true alignment, so none of the exceptions
above apply to it.
Exact-role checks see the true role. The Roleplayer is seen as "Roleplayer".
Token counts (Accountant) see the true total at the end of the night. The Roleplayer is seen as having 0 tokens,
even though they believe they have their fake role's tokens.
Visit-based results (Tracker, Lookout, Fortune Teller, Cartographer, Scout) are never changed by any of these.

=== PART 5: THE YAKUZA ===

R8 (Yakuza and the Katana)
- One random Yakuza starts with the Katana. The Yakuza share a private chat at night.
- Each night the Yakuza vote, at the same time, on who holds the Katana that night (and the next Day) and whom it
  attacks, if anyone. Both choices need a majority of living Yakuza; with two Yakuza alive, both must agree.
  Without a majority on a target, no attack happens; without a majority on a holder, the Katana doesn't move.
  A majority may move the Katana without attacking.
- The Katana attack is Standard and is dealt by whoever holds it at the end of the night. It is an action and a
  visit by that player (the new holder, if it moved that night): role-blocking them stops it, and Trackers see
  them visit the target. Moving or passing the Katana isn't an action: a role-block doesn't stop it (a blocked
  new holder still gets the Katana, but their attack fails), and it isn't a visit.
- The holder may also use their own role's night action.
- The holder appears Good to alignment checks that night (R19).
- The attacked player only learns they were attacked with the Katana, not the Yakuza role.
- At the end of the night, each Yakuza learns what actions the other Yakuza chose, but not their results
  (e.g. whether the Pharmacist's block worked) or whether a teammate was role-blocked.
- Role-blocked Yakuza still vote on the Katana's holder and target; the votes aren't actions.
- If the holder dies, the Katana passes to a random living Yakuza, if any; a holder who dies at night passes it on
  after that night's results. The living Yakuza are told who holds it now (and so learn that the holder died).

=== PART 6: ROLES ===

Every role lists the same fields. Defaults, unless a role says otherwise: Defense None, no tokens, appears as its
true alignment (R19), night action is a visit.

--- Village (Good) ---

Townsfolk (most villagers, helpful to the Village)

Vanilla Villager
  Night: none.

Investigative

Sheriff
  Night: may investigate one player. Learn Evil or Not Evil (alignment check, R19).

Tracker
  Night: may track one player. Learn whom they visited.

Lookout
  Night: may watch one player. Learn who visited them, not counting your own visit.

Seer
  Tokens: 1 seer token.
  Night: at the end of every night, you are told two random players other than yourself who were alive when the
  night began (players who die that night count, R10), and whether their alignments (Good/Neutral/Evil) are the
  same (alignment check, R19). Instead, you may spend a token to choose the
  two living players yourself (not including yourself). A chosen pair is a visit to both players; the random
  pair isn't a visit. A role-block stops both.

Fortune Teller
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn two numbers about that night, each labeled: how many players were
  visited (a player visited several times counts once), and how many players visited anyone (a player who visited
  several players counts once). This needs no action. Self-visits (R6) count in both numbers.
  Example: A holds the Katana, attacks B and also uses their own role's action on C, D visits B, and E protects
  themself. Visited: B, C and E, so 3. Visitors: A, D and E, so 3. Equal numbers don't mean nobody was visited
  twice.

Oracle
  Night: may guess one player's exact role (Astral Visit). At the end of the night, learn whether you were right.

Eavesdropper
  Night: may eavesdrop on one player. Only during the following Day (not the Night you eavesdrop), you read the contents of every private
  message they send or receive, as it is sent. Puppeted messages reach you as the puppet's (you aren't told about
  the puppeting). They aren't told.

Archivist
  Tokens: 1 archive token.
  Night: may spend the token to consult the archive. At the end of the night, let N be the number of players other
  than you who were alive when the night began (players who died that night count): you are shown N roles, in
  random order and without names, of which floor(0.5 * N) are real and the rest are fake. The real ones are the
  roles of floor(0.5 * N) of those players, chosen at random; a role appears as many times as it was drawn, so
  two drawn Vanilla Villagers show twice. This is an exact-role check (R19).
  Each fake is drawn at random from all the roles in these rules, including roles that are in the game, except
  that the result never shows a unique role (R2) twice.

Surveyor
  Tokens: 3 survey tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to survey one player other than yourself. The group is that player plus their nearest
  neighbor on each side in the circle (R11) among the players alive at the start of the night, skipping yourself
  and never counting anyone twice (so with only one or two other players alive, the group is smaller). You are
  told who was in the group and the exact role of one of them chosen at random, but not whose it is. Players who
  die that night can still be chosen. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Census Taker
  Night: may take a census around one player other than yourself (a visit to that player only).
  The program adds two other players drawn at random from everyone alive at the start of the night except you
  (players who die that night can be drawn; if fewer than two others are left, the group is smaller). It also
  draws at random whether to count Good or Evil players. You are told who was in the group, which alignment was
  counted, and how many of the group are of it. It counts true alignment and is not an alignment check (R19):
  the Katana holder, framed players and the Ex-Con count as what they really are, and
  Outsiders (e.g. the Roleplayer and the Ex-Con) count as Good. Neutral players are never
  counted, as either Good or Evil.

Coroner
  Tokens: 3 coroner tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to examine one player who died before the night began (not one who left the game, and not
  one who dies tonight). You learn their role, unless a Mortician cleaned them: then you learn only that. This is an
  Astral Visit (R6) and an exact-role check (R19).

Chronicler
  Tokens: 2 chronicler tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to mark one player other than yourself. This is a visit. The marked player isn't told.
  The mark lasts for the rest of the game, even after you die. If a marked player dies, at any time and of any
  cause, the announcement of their death also reveals their true role to everyone (an exact-role check, R19), and
  says they had been marked by a Chronicler (not by whom). A Mortician's clean beats the mark: a marked player who
  is cleaned has their role and will hidden, and the announcement says they had been marked but the clean hid their
  role. You can't mark a player you already marked. Marking a player another Chronicler already marked spends your
  token but adds nothing.

Auditor
  Night: may audit one player other than yourself. You learn every vote they cast during the Day just before this
  Night, in order: Yes or No on each nomination and Guilty or Innocent in each trial. If they cast none, you learn
  that. A doubled vote (Ballot Stuffer) shows as a single Guilty or Innocent.

Juror
  Night: may name two different players other than yourself (dead players allowed; Astral Visit). You learn how many
  times they voted the same way, over every Day so far, counted separately for trial votes (Guilty/Innocent) and
  nomination votes (Yes/No), e.g. "the same way in 3 of 4 trial votes and 5 of 9 nomination votes". Only votes
  both of them cast count, and not votes on the nomination or trial of either of them. A doubled vote (Ballot
  Stuffer) counts once. You learn only the totals, not which votes they agreed on.

Bloodhound
  Tokens: 2 scent tokens.
  Night: at the end of every night, code draws three random players other than you from those alive at the start of
  the night, and you learn their names and how many Attacks (R3) they have made in total this game, tonight's
  included, whether or not the Attacks killed anyone. Each player's Katana attacks, shots, alert or trap hits and
  so on all count; a role-blocked attack never happened, so it doesn't. This needs no action and a role-block
  doesn't stop it.
  Night: may also spend a token to track one player other than yourself: they take one of the three places that
  night and code draws the other two. A role-block stops the tracking (R9) but not the result.

Scrutineer
  Night: may scrutinize one player other than yourself who voted in the Day's trials (Astral Visit). Code adds two
  random other players who voted in those trials (never you), and you learn the three names and, for each trial of
  the Day just before this Night, how many of the three voted Guilty, e.g. "2 in the trial of Erin; 0 in the trial
  of Frank". You don't learn which of them voted which way. A doubled vote (Ballot Stuffer) counts once. If there
  was no trial that Day, you learn that.

Profiler
  Tokens: 3 profile tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to profile one player other than yourself. You learn three different roles, exactly one
  of which is that player's true role. Of the other two, one is drawn at random from the roles of the other players
  alive at the start of the night (including players who die that night, but not yourself), and the other from the
  roles that no player in the game has. At least one of the three is a Good role and at least one is not Good (Evil
  or Neutral), so a result never settles the player's alignment on its own; which of the two supplies the missing
  side is random. When no role fits a draw, that one is drawn from all roles in these rules instead. The three are
  different and listed in alphabetical order. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Cartographer
  Tokens: 2 map tokens.
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn the sizes of that night's visit groups. Link two players whenever one
  visited the other that night (R6). Direction is ignored: A visiting B links them exactly as B visiting A
  would. A group is a set of players linked to each other, directly or through other players. Every player alive at
  the start of the night (including players who die that night) is in exactly one group, so a player who visited no
  one and was visited by no one is a group of 1, and a self-visit links no one. You learn only the sizes, largest
  first (e.g. "4, 2, 1, 1, 1"). This needs no action and a role-block doesn't stop it.
  Night: may also spend a token to map one player (Astral Visit; yourself allowed): at the end of the night you also
  learn the names of everyone in that player's group. A role-block stops the map (R9) but not the sizes.
  Your own actions never visit anyone, so they never link you to anyone.

Scout
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn the names of three players (you may be one of them) who were each in a
  different visit group that night. Groups are as for the Cartographer (visit direction is ignored). The names are
  drawn like this: a random player, then a random player outside the groups already drawn from, and so on, so a big
  group is more likely to come up than a small one. If there were fewer than three groups, you learn one name per
  group and how many groups there were. This needs no action and a role-block doesn't stop it. You never visit
  anyone.

Insomniac
  Tokens: 2 insomniac tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to stay awake. At the end of the night, you learn the roles of up to 3 players who visited
  someone that night (R6; a visit to themselves counts), but not who they are: if more than 3 players visited, 3 of
  them are drawn at random. The roles are listed in alphabetical order, and a role shows twice if two of those
  players have it. If fewer than 3 players visited, you learn all of their roles, and if nobody visited, you learn
  that. Players who visited and then died that night count. Only visits count: an action that isn't a visit (e.g.
  an Astral Visit or a Veteran's alert) doesn't. Staying awake is not a visit. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Accountant
  Night: may audit one player. Learn how many tokens they have in total at the end of the night, after any they
  spent that night and any a Magpie stole (token count, R19). You learn only the total, not what kind of tokens
  they are.
  If their role changed at the end of this night, the role just before the change counts.

Combat

Medic
  Tokens: 2 medic tokens.
  Night: may protect one player other than yourself, giving them Standard Defense. Spend 1 token to give Strong
  Defense instead, and 1 token to protect yourself instead of another player; the two can be combined (so
  protecting yourself costs 1 token with Standard Defense and 2 with Strong).

Trapper
  Night: may place a trap on one player other than yourself and other than the player your trap is already on, or
  may remove your trap (removing it isn't a visit). You have one trap at a time; a new trap replaces the old one at
  once. Traps last even after you die. A trap is armed from the next night on: the first time a
  non-Village player visits the trapped player on a later night, the trap is used up and that visitor is dealt a
  Strong Attack. If several non-Village players visit that night, one of them, chosen at random, is hit. You learn
  that your trap went off, and nothing else (not who, nor whether it killed).

Vigilante
  Tokens: 3 vigilante tokens.
  Night: may shoot one player: 1 token for a Basic Attack, 2 for Standard, 3 for Strong. If your shot kills them,
  you also learn their role (exact-role check, R19).

Veteran
  Tokens: 3 alert tokens.
  You can't be role-blocked.
  Night: may spend a token to go on alert (not a visit, R6, so nothing that reacts to visits counts it). While on
  alert you have Standard Defense and you deal a Strong Attack to every player who visits you that night, whatever
  their faction (a role-blocker who visits you is attacked too), however many there are. Astral Visits aren't
  visits, so they aren't attacked. At the end of the night you learn whether anyone visited you and, if so, how
  many, and whether your attack on each of them succeeded, but nothing about who they were.

Misc

Prosecutor
  Tokens: 2 prosecutor tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to prosecute someone. At the start of the next Day, before anyone speaks, the moderator
  announces that someone is being prosecuted; this counts as a successful nomination and they go to trial. It
  counts toward the Day's three-nomination limit, an execution ends the Day as usual, and it can combine with a
  Clerk's rig. If the trial needs a "nominator", the moderator picks a random player.

Party Animal

  Night: may visit one player, role-blocking them.

Philanthropist

Outsiders (Village roles: Good, and win with the Village, but the role helps the Village less or can hurt it)

Roleplayer

Ex-Con

  Night: every night you visit a random player other than yourself, and you aren't told whom. A role-block stops

Cardinal

Grunt
  Night: none of its own.

Pharmacist

Ritualist

Puppeteer
  Tokens: 1 puppet token.
  Night: may spend a token to puppet any player for the following Day (puppeting yourself changes nothing). That
  Day, they are told they are being puppeted, and they can't chat or see private messages; nobody else is told. You
  chat publicly and privately in their place (including seeing their private messages) and can set their claim,
  which appears in the ledger as theirs; that is all you can do for them. They still nominate, vote and so on as
  normal. It lasts one Day.

Fabricator
  Tokens: 1 fabricator token.
  Night: may visit one non-Yakuza player to frame them (no token needed): that night they appear Evil to
  alignment checks (R19); other results are unchanged. On the same visit, you may spend a token to forge that

Clerk
  Tokens: 1 clerk token.
  Night: may spend a token to rig the next Day's votes. On a rigged Day, anyone successfully nominated is executed.
  The Guilty/Innocent vote still happens; if a majority votes Guilty, the rig is not announced, otherwise it is

Smuggler
  Immune to role-blocks.
  Tokens: 2 swap tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to swap two different living players (yourself included) for the night (R23). You visit

Ballot Stuffer
  Tokens: 2 ballot tokens.
  Night: may spend a token so that during the following Day your vote counts twice in every Guilty/Innocent trial

Fixer

Each Neutral player is their own faction (R2).

Arsonist

  Win: only alone (not even with another Arsonist).
  Night: may douse one player, or ignite (Astral Visit), dealing a Strong Attack to every doused player. A doused

  players are never told. Igniting uses up every douse: players who survive it are no longer doused.

Jester
  Defense: Basic. Appears: Evil to the Sheriff.

  Win: iff you are hanged during a Day (other daytime deaths don't count). You lose if the game ends with you

  Revenge: if you are hanged, the following night a random Guilty voter from your trial who was alive when that

Executioner
  Defense: Basic. Appears: Evil to the Sheriff.
  Never blocks wins (R1).
  At the start you get a random target: any player except yourself.
  Win: iff your target is hanged during a Day while you are alive (other daytime deaths don't count). You lose if

  On winning: the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game. Leaving works exactly like dying (you
  leave the circle for good) except it doesn't count as a death. The following night, a random Guilty voter from
  the trial who was alive when that night began (not you, since you left) is dealt a Divine Attack (Astral Visit). If nobody voted
  Guilty, nothing happens.
  If your target dies any other way, or leaves the game, you become a Jester.

Bounty Hunter
  Tokens: 1 attack token. Never blocks wins (R1).
  At the start you get 3 random targets: any players except yourself.
  Night: may spend the token to deal a Strong Attack to one player.
  A bounty on a target is claimed if they die by your attack or are hanged during a Day while your vote counted as
  Guilty. If a target dies any other way (or leaves the game), that bounty is lost. Night deaths are simultaneous
  (R10): a target you kill on the night you die still counts.
  Win: iff you claim 2 bounties. If you are alive then, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game
  (leaving works as for the Executioner). If you have died, you still win and nothing is revealed.
  Lose: once you can no longer claim 2 bounties; if you are alive, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave
  the game.

Magpie
  Defense: Basic. Never blocks wins (R1). Random setups include a Magpie only if at least a third of the roles have tokens.
  Night: may steal a token from another player (a visit). It happens at the end of the night, after that night's

  Win: iff you steal tokens from 3 different players (a second steal from the same player takes nothing). If you

  that night, you still win and nothing is revealed.

Vulture
  Win: alone, if you are alive at the start of a Day (after the night's deaths) and max(floor(N/4), 2) or fewer
  players are alive, counting yourself, where N is the number of players at the start of the game. The game then
  ends at once and everyone else loses (wins already earned by roles that never block wins still count, R1).
  Night: none.
  Day: at the start of each Day, you learn a role for each player who died since the previous Day began (during that

For each kill also set `by` to the player whose action killed them (the trap's owner for a trap) and katana=true for the Katana attack; these are recorded for analysis, never shown. Don't tell() deaths to all. Code tells each player who dies tonight that they were attacked and died, with the kill's cause, at the end of the night; you tell every attacked player who survived, and a player who died about any other Attack on them tonight, failed ones included (R3, R20 step 5). Tell each role-blocked player that they were role-blocked, even one with no night action or who chose not to act (R9); a role-blocker learns only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked (R9). Write private results in the present, about tonight ('You were role-blocked tonight'), never 'last night': they are delivered at the end of this night. Every player who used an ability gets a private result line, even when nothing else happened (e.g. 'You went on alert. 1 alert token left.'), stating any tokens they have left, except where a role note below says otherwise (e.g. code tells them, so don't tell() them a second result). Code tells the Yakuza which actions each of them chose and the Katana's holder and target (R8), so don't tell() them that; role-blocked Yakuza's Katana votes still count. Only the attacker learns whether the Katana attack succeeded: tell them. Update token counts for any tokens spent. Before end_phase, call record_visits once with every visit that happened tonight (R6, R20 steps 1-2), as [visitor, target] pairs, a self-visit as [X, X] (an empty list if there were none). Easy to miss: the Katana holder visits the Katana target (R8) besides any visit from their own role's action; automatic visits (the Ex-Con's); a Seer's chosen pair is a visit to both players. - A Clerk who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the rig_vote op, which spends the token; code executes tomorrow's accused regardless of the vote.

A per-day list of who sent private messages would have helped, since the ledger showed "none yet" throughout.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to send a private message to Bob or Erin to test their claims without publicly signalling my mark, and the interface gave me no clear confirmation that a private channel was usable or what it would cost compared with public chat. I also wanted a way to ask the moderator a direct question about the vote count on Day 4, since Grace and Erin disagreed about the Day 3 tally and I had no neutral way to resolve it.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The Day 2 claims repeated the same entries several times for Alice, Bob and Erin, which made the ledger noisy. Grace's claim on Day 4 contained a stated vote that contradicted the announced totals, and her correction arrived only after she was already nominated. The Day 3 hang of Dave with four Guilty votes was consistent with the totals, but the nomination count of four Yes out of five left one voter ambiguous to everyone. Nothing else looked broken.
answers.suggestions: Show each player's own vote in their private reminder and in the ledger as a single line, labelled as their claim versus the announced totals, so contradictions can be checked immediately. Publish speaking budget and the price table at the start of each turn, not only in the setup text. Allow a short neutral moderator answer to factual questions about announced counts, so disputes over the tally can be settled without a vote. Keep the notepad limit (300 words) but tell players how much is already used in the same prompt.

answers.confusing_rules: Two points were unclear. First, how the Clerk's rig interacts with the Day's nominations and trials was not spelled out in the night prompt, so I could not plan a rigged Day with confidence. Second, the speaking budget numbers were given only as a formula and a short summary, and I could not easily tell how much budget I had left when I was deciding whether a message was affordable.
answers.missing_information: I had trouble keeping track of the public vote record. Each player's stated votes were spread across several claim lines, and corrections (such as Grace's Day 3 correction) were posted inline. A compact per-Day table of nominations, trial votes and totals, with each player's stated vote next to it, would have helped. I also could not see my own remaining Clerk token count in the prompt header; I had to rely on my notepad.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to see the night action menu in full before choosing, including whether a Clerk rig was offered on Night 2 and what it would have cost. I wanted to privately confirm my teammate status and whether any other Yakuza existed, but the interface gave no sign of that beyond the header. I also could not review the public ledger's claim history in one place to check which players had changed their stated votes.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing clearly broken. The final ledger and totals were consistent with the announced counts. One oddity: the Day 4 trial result (3 Guilty, 1 Innocent of 4 votes) matched the living count, but the ledger still showed Grace's Day 3 votes as they had been first stated, which made the record look contradictory until her correction was posted. Also, Dave's Clerk role was revealed only because of the Chronicler mark, which is by design but meant a Clerk's death looked like a Chronicler's success.
answers.suggestions: Show the full vote record (nominations and trial votes with each player's stated vote and the totals) in the header each Day. Show remaining tokens for each player's own role in the night prompt. State explicitly how a rig is announced if the Guilty majority still forms, since that rule was only implied. For a sole surviving Yakuza, say whether night-chat or teammate-death notices are shown, so the player knows the team has ended.

answers.confusing_rules: Whether a Katana holder's attack counts as a "night action" when a player claims "no action." Dave's claims said "no action" on nights when the moderator's log shows a Katana vote and attack. A Vanilla claim seems to ignore a Katana vote, which may be a real loophole or just a wording issue. Also unclear: how a Chronicler mark's reveal works when the Chronicler's own claim is the only source.
answers.missing_information: Nothing in my view of the game showed each player's speaking budget or price table, so I couldn't plan how much I could say. The public ledger's "earlier" claim history mixes several days into one line per player, which made it hard to see when each claim changed. A per-player, per-day record of claims and votes would help. I also never saw the Katana holder or the Yakuza's identities, so the Katana's mechanics were only inferable from the moderator's night log.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to check Grace's and Carol's stories privately before voting, but no private messages were sent in this game ("none yet"). I didn't try to send one, so I can't say whether it was blocked. I'd have liked a way to ask one player a direct question privately without it being visible to the whole table.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Grace's Day 3 claim contained a self-contradiction ("Innocent on Dave's trial (no, see Day 3 votes)") that only the later correction resolved. The announced totals for Dave's nomination (4 Yes) and trial (4 Guilty) were only consistent with Grace's corrected votes, so one player's public record was wrong for a full day. Day 2 also filled with repeated "agree, no nomination" posts that added no information, possibly a side effect of the speaking budget or the lack of early results.
answers.suggestions: Show a compact vote and claim log with the Day number on each entry, so players can verify a changed claim without reading the full history. Post the speaking budget and price table each turn so players can see when a message will cost too much. Consider giving Night 1 results to more roles, since with no early information Day 2 reduced to filler.

answers.confusing_rules: I never found out whether dead players can still speak in public chat or post claims. The game shows me no prompts after death, so I couldn't test it. The Katana rules say a Yakuza holder appears Good to alignment checks, but nothing tells a dead Archivist-type role whether its own results still count. The Clerk-reveal and Chronicler-mark rules were clear once I saw them applied, though the exact timing of a marked death's reveal (announced at once vs. at the start of the Day) was only clear from the example.
answers.missing_information: As Frank, I died on Night 1 and never saw any Katana holder identity, so I had no way to know who the Yakuza were. I also never learned whether my Archivist token could have been used on Night 1 after I was attacked. It would help to know, on a death, whether the dead player's last visible role claim or token balance is shown to the living. The public ledger's claim history was hard to read: entries like "earlier: ... ; Day 3: ..." are mixed with corrected votes (Grace's Day 3 correction), so it was easy to lose track of which vote a player actually cast.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to know whether a dead player could still post a final message or argue for a player during the Day after death. I also wanted a clean per-player vote history that marks corrections explicitly, instead of having to reconstruct it from the totals and claim text.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The claim summary for Grace read "D3: No on nomination of Dave, Innocent on Dave's trial (no, see Day 3 votes)", which contradicted the announced totals (Yes on nomination and Guilty on trial). The correction came from Grace herself, not from the ledger, so the public record was wrong until a player fixed it. The ledger also kept stale entries for Erin (Day 3 "nominated Dave") next to later entries, which made the nomination counts harder to check. I did not see any moderator-level rule violation, but the record-keeping was messy.
answers.suggestions: Show the ledger's vote history as one clean table per player (nomination votes and trial votes by Day), and mark any correction as a correction with the original value. State explicitly whether dead players may speak or nominate, and whether they can still post a last message after death. Announce on death whether the dead player had any unspent tokens. Also consider a short notice when a Katana holder moves, so living players can see the Yakuza's hand without guessing.

answers.confusing_rules: The Arsonist rules were the hardest part. "Douse" and "ignite" are both listed as night actions, and the prompt never states whether ignite needs a specific number of living doused players, whether dead doused players count, or whether a douse ends when the Arsonist dies. My notes assumed "three living doused," which the rules don't spell out. The Chronicler and Coroner "astral" wording also differs from ordinary visits, and I had to reread R6 and R18 to see what counts as a visit.
answers.missing_information: I never had a live list of which of my doused players were still alive and doused, so I tracked it by hand. The Arsonist's night prompt should show the current doused list and the living doused count. I also had no view of the Katana holder and target until the reveal. Vote totals were announced without voter names, which is expected, but a private end-of-Day reminder of my own recorded votes would have prevented my Day 3 vote-record mistake.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to know whether ignite was available on Night 3, when I had two living doused players (Erin and Bob) plus one dead (Alice). The interface gave no way to check before choosing, so I just doused again. I also wanted the living Yakuza count at the start of each Night, since it decides how dangerous a Village hang is for an Arsonist.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing clearly broken. My Day 3 vote was misrecorded in my own notes and the ledger initially showed "Innocent" on Dave's trial, while my real vote was Guilty; the totals only fit the corrected version. The win check ended the game correctly. One oddity: after Dave's Day 3 hanging, no one was killed on Night 3, so the Yakuza had no Katana holder left to act before the game ended on my hang.
answers.suggestions: 1) For the Arsonist, show the living doused count and the ignite condition in the night prompt, and state whether dead doused players count. 2) Give each player a private end-of-Day summary of their own announced votes so vote claims can be checked. 3) When a vote is corrected, post the corrected vote publicly so the ledger matches the totals. 4) Add a short reminder in each Day prompt of the three-failed-nomination and Day-end rules, since I had to check them twice.

answers.confusing_rules:
1) Census Taker group (R-Census). The text says the census is "around one player". I read that as the target plus two random others drawn from everyone alive at the start of the night except the Census Taker, and both results fit that reading (N1: Bob plus Dave and Frank; N2: Dave plus Erin and Grace). "Around" sounds like it means circle neighbours, the way it does for the Surveyor and Diviner. Players could reasonably misread it.
2) Census results with a Neutral in the group. On N2 the result was 1 of 3 Good, with Dave Evil, Erin Good and Grace Neutral. That is correct, but a Good count lumps Neutral and Evil together, so a non-Good player could be Neutral. The rules imply this but never spell it out. Players kept treating "non-Good" as "Yakuza". It happened to be true for Dave, but the same reasoning would have misled them about Grace.
3) Setup balance. The setup says "fewer Yakuza tend to get stronger roles", yet the single Yakuza got Clerk, a one-use role with no night action of its own. I followed the draw, but that guideline doesn't seem to have been applied here.
4) R14 stall rule. I checked whether Night 3 (no deaths) mattered. It didn't, because Dave was hanged on Day 3. The wording "three previous Nights and three previous Days" is still easy to misread as a combined count of six phases.
answers.missing_information:
1) My log showed only vote totals, not how each player voted. On Day 4 the trial turned on Grace's vote record. She first claimed No/Innocent on Dave, then said it was Yes/Guilty. I couldn't check which version was true, or whether Dave's claimed No was honest. The moderator should have the full per-voter record, even though players must not see it.
2) I couldn't see anyone's speaking budget, so I couldn't tell whether the repeated near-identical posts on Day 2 were a choice or a result of budget limits.
3) I had no running state summary. I tracked by hand who the Arsonist had doused (Alice, who was already dead, then Erin and Bob), how many tokens each player had left (Clerk 1 unused, Coroner 1, Chronicler 0), and who held the Katana. A per-night state table would make errors much less likely.
4) No record of how the setup was generated (Yakuza count roll, balance score), so I couldn't confirm the 1 Yakuza + 1 Neutral + 5 Village split was meant to be balanced.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt:
1) Add a note to the census result saying that Neutral players are also non-Good under a Good count. Only the standard text was available.
2) Check claimed votes against the real ones during Grace's trial. This was for my own consistency, not to tell players.
3) Flag a malformed claim-ledger entry (see bugs). There was no moderator tool to annotate or reject it.
answers.bugs_or_oddities:
1) Grace's Day 4 claim-ledger entry contained garbled, self-contradicting text: "D3: No on nomination of Dave, Innocent on Dave's trial (no, see Day 3 votes). D4: No on nomination of Grace (I was nominated)". The ledger accepts free text that contradicts itself and records it as a claim.
2) Day 2 was eight rounds of nearly identical "waiting for Day 3" posts, about 50 messages with almost no new content. The Day only ended at the 8-round cap. Some posts referred to things that hadn't happened yet: Erin asked Carol on Day 2 whether she had marked anyone on Night 2, which was still to come. This doesn't break any rule, but the Day was mostly wasted.
3) Alice's Night 2 census (Dave, Erin, Grace: 1 of 3 Good) was delivered on the night she died. That is correct under R10, but the result could never reach anyone, because wills can't be updated at night.
4) The Clerk's rig token went unused, and with a lone Yakuza the Katana vote was trivial. This isn't a bug, but the Yakuza side was very weak.
5) Arsonist: Grace never ignited, though she had living doused targets from Night 3 on. That was a strategy choice, not a bug. I double-checked that Good players are never told they were doused, and that the Arsonist correctly blocked a Village win after Dave died.
6) Everything else resolved as written: census counts, Coroner results, Chronicler reveal on hanging, majority thresholds (4/6, 3/5, 3/4) and the final win check.
answers.suggestions:
1) Give the moderator a hidden per-voter vote log and a per-night state panel: tokens left, douse list, Katana holder, traps and marks.
2) Validate claim-ledger entries. Reject or flag claims that contradict themselves, and possibly show a diff when a player revises an earlier claim.
3) Clarify the Census Taker text: the two extra players are random, not circle neighbours, and under a Good count Neutrals are included in the non-Good part.
4) Apply the "fewer Yakuza get stronger roles" rule more strongly, for example by not giving a lone Yakuza a role with no night action.
5) Discourage zero-content Days. Either end the Day sooner when a full round brings no new claims or votes, or raise the cost of repeated public messages, so a Day 2 like this one doesn't run all 8 rounds.
6) Let a player who dies at night have their result from that night added to their will automatically (as an option), so results like Alice's last census aren't lost.

title: Post-game lessons: tips players wish they'd known, and how past tips went

task:
If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

You were also given tips from past games (in your instructions). Which of them went especially well or badly for you or others this game? List only tips that clearly mattered (or none): helped, hurt (followed it and it backfired, or it was predictable to opponents), or wrong (it is false or contradicts the rules), and why, concretely.

lessons.applies_to: Coroner, Mortician and other astral-check roles
lessons.tip: Spend the astral check on a dead player early (Night 2 at the latest) and post the exact role in your first Day speech. A verified role on a dead Village player (here Frank, then Alice) cut the suspect list in half and was the only hard evidence in the game.

Before a hang, list which players have no verifiable result at all and ask each of them for one checkable fact. Day 4's hang of Grace rested on silence and a misstated vote record. Silence alone is not a mechanic; a concrete mismatch between a claimed vote and the announced totals is.

A Chronicler mark plus a death reveal is a free role check. Mark only on evidence you can state, and if a marked player dies, the reveal is a strong public fact to build the next Day's case on. Carol's mark on Dave verified a Clerk Yakuza and was the game's clearest signal.

Compare nomination and trial totals against the claimed votes of everyone before voting. Grace's self-correction showed that a player who misstates their own vote record can be checked against the 4-Yes and 4-Guilty totals; use that arithmetic rather than tone.

When a Day is spent saying wait, name a deadline for results and a default nominee. Day 2 ran with almost everyone repeating 'no nomination until Day 3', which gave the Katana two free kills and let claims sit unchallenged.

tips_feedback.tip: Post your role, target and exact result in your first speech after getting it.
tips_feedback.why: Bob's Coroner claim was posted with a Night 2 plan and then a verified result, and later results were checked against Alice's census, which made it credible.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit.
tips_feedback.why: Bob's Dave argument used the census count (2 of 3 Good) and the Clerk reveal to make the case; it was accepted and was correct.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit.
tips_feedback.why: Voting on Grace rested on silence and a vote-record mismatch that later turned out to be a misstatement, not a lie, so the mechanical fit was thinner than it looked.

tips_feedback.tip: Answer a direct question about your night action in one plain sentence the first time it is asked.
tips_feedback.why: Night actions were stated plainly on Days 2 to 4, which avoided suspicion from the evasion pattern.

I'm thinking through what honestly happened in the game—the Village won, with Bob and Carol among the winners—to form genuine lessons learned.

Dave was the Clerk and also Yakuza, hanged after Carol's Chronicler mark triggered a role reveal on his death, while Grace was actually the Arsonist (not Yakuza) and got hanged too, though as a lone-win neutral that doesn't count as a Village win alongside Frank and Alice who were Village. lessons.tip: Before posting any vote or correction, write your exact nomination and trial votes in your notepad and check them against the announced totals. I misstated my Day 3 votes (said No/Innocent when I had voted Yes/Guilty), and the correction cost me credibility when the table was already split. A self-inflicted mismatch looks like a lie even when it is an honest error.

Silence is a liability. Being quiet for two Days with no role or result got me nominated 'for silence' on Day 4. Post a short, concrete status each Day (role or no role, what you did, what you're watching) so nobody can build a case from your absence.

Build a Yakuza read from mechanics, not volume. The Day 3 hang was right because Bob's Coroner result on Frank and Alice's census both pointed at Dave, and Carol's Chronicler mark on Dave came back as a Clerk. Checking which claims share a common mechanical source is what separated true from false here.

Douses persist across nights until an ignite, but a doused player who dies no longer counts toward the 3 living doused needed. Count only living doused players, and plan ignite timing around deaths. Dousing Village players who are being watched by Coroner, Chronicler or Census Taker risks drawing attention, so keep the douse pattern quiet and don't announce it.

A Neutral who is only dousing or waiting to ignite should choose one clear public story early (for example Vanilla with no night action), and keep it. My silence plus changing vote records made me the hang target when Yakuza were already losing.

tips_feedback.tip: Vote as you said you would and explain any switch first; a mismatch with the totals is a lead.
tips_feedback.why: The 4 Yes and 4 Guilty totals were used to catch my misstated Day 3 votes. Nobody could ignore the mismatch, and I had to correct it publicly.

tips_feedback.why: I did not state a role or night result until Day 4, after I was already the target of a nomination for silence. Delay read as hiding even though I had no information to share.

task:
If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

You were also given tips from past games (in your instructions). Which of them went especially well or badly for you or others this game? List only tips that clearly mattered (or none): helped, hurt (followed it and it backfired, or it was predictable to opponents), or wrong (it is false or contradicts the rules), and why, concretely.

lessons.tip: Mark the player you most suspect on a reasoned basis, not out of a single census. A mark pays off only if that player dies, and it reveals their true role to everyone. My Night 2 mark on Dave was lucky, and my Night 3 mark on Bob had no stated reason, so it could have wasted a token and cast doubt on me.

Check each claimed vote against the announced totals before you accept or attack it. Nomination counts can't be altered, so a claimed No that doesn't fit the Yes count is a clean lie check. Grace's false vote record came out only because the arithmetic was checked.

Silence alone is not a reason to nominate. I nominated Grace on Day 4 mainly for not stating a role, and Grace was a Neutral Arsonist who was not Yakuza. Before nominating, name a mechanical contradiction, not a missing claim.

Track the Arsonist's douse pattern. Doused players are not told when they are Good, so the Night 1 to 3 douse targets (Alice, Erin, Bob) were a strong clue that the douser was a Neutral building toward an ignite. Ask who was doused and who visited them, then nominate the visitor if the pattern fits.

Coroner and Census claims that can be cross-checked are worth more than any single claim. Ask which claims interlock (a census group containing a dead player, a coroner exam of that player) and check those interlocks before any hang. The Day 3 hang rested on one unverifiable coroner result and was right only by luck.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit.
tips_feedback.why: Forcing a mechanical reason exposed Grace's inconsistent vote record and the Day 4 vote count mismatch, which made the final hang clearer.

tips_feedback.tip: A mismatch with the totals is a lead, never a hang on its own.
tips_feedback.why: Grace's corrected vote record and the 4-Yes count together were the real evidence. The mismatch alone did not decide the vote.

tips_feedback.tip: Hunt Neutral killers deliberately and hang the best suspect before the final two.
tips_feedback.why: The Day 4 hang of Grace removed a Neutral Arsonist, which did not hurt the Village, but I hung her for silence rather than for a Neutral read. The tip is incomplete: a hang for a non-Yakuza Neutral can also end the game early.

tips_feedback.tip: Never announce tonight's target, in public or by PM.
tips_feedback.why: I publicly announced my Night 2 mark on Dave on Day 3. That made Dave the obvious target and turned the trial into a vote on my mark rather than on evidence. The table was already thin, so it likely helped the Yakuza's case against me.

output.reason: Answered with reusable lessons and tip verdicts from this game's play, leaving unused fields empty as instructed.

reasoning:
This is a reflective question, so I'll respond using the structured output format, focusing on lessons and tips_feedback along with the standard notepad, reason, and feedback fields, leaving the rest empty. The lessons should be concrete and reusable.

Thinking through the game as Carol: Dave turned out to be Yakuza (Clerk cover, held the Katana), Grace was the neutral Arsonist, while Bob and Erin were Good roles, so the Village ultimately won. My mark on Dave at N2 was based only on Alice's census but proved correct, while marking Bob at N3 without real justification was a weaker, unreasoned move—marks should be used purposefully as a reveal tool tied to someone I'm already planning to vote against. The Day 4 nomination of Grace over "silence" was similarly weak reasoning, even though it happened to target the Arsonist correctly.

I'm noting that hanging a neutral like Grace without solid evidence is risky, and that vote arithmetic matters—checking claimed vote counts against the actual totals (like the 4-of-5 Yes on Dave's nomination) exposes inconsistencies and liars. I'm also thinking about how an Arsonist's dousing pattern leaves visible traces to Lookouts, Trackers, or Fortune Tellers, since doused players are only informed if they aren't Good, so tracking those visits could help identify the Arsonist. Finally, I'm reinforcing that the Chronicler's mark is most valuable when placed on a strongly suspected player, since the resulting reveal at death—as happened with Dave—gives the village crucial confirmation, and that Coroner examinations of dead roles provide strong corroborating evidence.

Now I'm reviewing how well each piece of advice performed: the "name a concrete mechanical fit before voting Guilty" tip helped justify the Dave hang, the "never announce tonight's target" tip was technically broken but didn't backfire, answering direct questions plainly worked well, keeping a written will of planned targets was useful, and the vote-mismatch tip was validated by exposing Grace's miscount—though the advice to hunt Neutral killers deliberately is less clearly validated since Grace's hanging outcome was ambiguous. I'm deciding to leave most structured output fields empty since there isn't much else notable to report, keeping the feedback and notepad fields blank and just filling in the lessons that actually proved useful.
